claim: Climate-driven expansions of ocean hypoxic zones are predicted to concentrate pelagic fish in oxygenated surface layers.
source: Climate-driven expansions of ocean hypoxic zones are predicted to concentrate pelagic fish in oxygenated surface layers, but how expanding hypoxia and fisheries will interact to affect threatened pelagic sharks remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about predictions in the scientific literature regarding hypoxic zones and pelagic fish behavior.

claim: Blue shark maximum dive depths decreased in the eastern tropical Atlantic oxygen minimum zone.
source: Here, analysis of satellite-tracked blue sharks and environmental modelling in the eastern tropical Atlantic oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) shows shark maximum dive depths decreased due to combined effects of decreasing dissolved oxygen (DO) at depth, high sea surface temperatures, and increased surface-layer net primary production.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from satellite tracking analysis and environmental modeling.

claim: Blue shark maximum dive depths decreased due to combined effects of decreasing dissolved oxygen at depth, high sea surface temperatures, and increased surface-layer net primary production.
source: Here, analysis of satellite-tracked blue sharks and environmental modelling in the eastern tropical Atlantic oxygen minimum zone (OMZ) shows shark maximum dive depths decreased due to combined effects of decreasing dissolved oxygen (DO) at depth, high sea surface temperatures, and increased surface-layer net primary production.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the causal factors identified through analysis.

claim: Multiple factors associated with climate-driven deoxygenation contributed to blue shark vertical habitat compression.
source: Multiple factors associated with climate-driven deoxygenation contributed to blue shark vertical habitat compression, potentially increasing their vulnerability to surface fisheries.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the study findings.

claim: Climate-driven deoxygenation potentially increases blue shark vulnerability to surface fisheries.
source: Multiple factors associated with climate-driven deoxygenation contributed to blue shark vertical habitat compression, potentially increasing their vulnerability to surface fisheries.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the habitat compression findings.

claim: Greater intensity of longline fishing effort occurred above the OMZ compared to adjacent waters.
source: Greater intensity of longline fishing effort occurred above the OMZ compared to adjacent waters.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Higher shark catches were associated with strong DO gradients.
source: Higher shark catches were associated with strong DO gradients, suggesting potential aggregation along suitable DO gradients contributed to habitat compression and higher fishing-induced mortality.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from catch data analysis.

claim: Potential aggregation along suitable DO gradients contributed to habitat compression and higher fishing-induced mortality.
source: Higher shark catches were associated with strong DO gradients, suggesting potential aggregation along suitable DO gradients contributed to habitat compression and higher fishing-induced mortality.
evidence: This is presented as a suggested mechanism based on the catch data findings.

claim: Fisheries controls to counteract deoxygenation effects on shark catches will be needed as oceans continue warming.
source: Fisheries controls to counteract deoxygenation effects on shark catches will be needed as oceans continue warming.
evidence: This is a management recommendation stated in the abstract.

claim: Dissolved oxygen content of the global ocean is declining due to sea temperature warming, increased stratification, and changing circulation.
source: Dissolved oxygen (DO) content of the global ocean is declining (ocean deoxygenation) due to sea temperature warming, increased stratification, and changing circulation, and the interactions of these processes with hypoxia-inducing biological activity (Keeling et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Watson, 2016; Schmidtko et al., 2017; Breitburg et al., 2018; Levin, 2018; Laffoley and Baxter, 2019; Stramma and Schmidtko, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to the scientific literature.

claim: Permanent oxygen minimum zones are present in all the world's ocean basins.
source: Permanent oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) are present in all the world's ocean basins and occur where DO reaches low (hypoxic) levels of <0.45–1.00 ml O2 l−1 in the depth range ~200–800 m (Keeling et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; for oxygen units used see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: OMZs occur where DO reaches low (hypoxic) levels of <0.45–1.00 ml O2 l−1 in the depth range ~200–800 m.
source: Permanent oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) are present in all the world's ocean basins and occur where DO reaches low (hypoxic) levels of <0.45–1.00 ml O2 l−1 in the depth range ~200–800 m (Keeling et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; for oxygen units used see Materials and methods).
evidence: This defines OMZs with citation support.

claim: Ocean deoxygenation has resulted in horizontal and vertical expansions of OMZs.
source: Ocean deoxygenation has resulted in horizontal and vertical expansions of OMZs with the prospect of profound effects on marine biota because long-term DO declines are particularly acute in OMZs (Stramma et al., 2008; Gilly et al., 2013; Breitburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Long-term DO declines are particularly acute in OMZs.
source: Ocean deoxygenation has resulted in horizontal and vertical expansions of OMZs with the prospect of profound effects on marine biota because long-term DO declines are particularly acute in OMZs (Stramma et al., 2008; Gilly et al., 2013; Breitburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Levels of DO have a major role in structuring marine ecosystems.
source: Levels of DO have a major role in structuring marine ecosystems (Grantham et al., 2004; Ekau et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Levin and Le Bris, 2015; Breitburg et al., 2018; Penn et al., 2018; Laffoley and Baxter, 2019) because the vast majority of organisms have a low hypoxic threshold, where concentrations of ~1.35–2.70 ml O2 l−1 cause hypoxic stress (Vaquer-Sunyer and Duarte, 2008; Ekau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The vast majority of organisms have a low hypoxic threshold, where concentrations of ~1.35–2.70 ml O2 l−1 cause hypoxic stress.
source: Levels of DO have a major role in structuring marine ecosystems (Grantham et al., 2004; Ekau et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Levin and Le Bris, 2015; Breitburg et al., 2018; Penn et al., 2018; Laffoley and Baxter, 2019) because the vast majority of organisms have a low hypoxic threshold, where concentrations of ~1.35–2.70 ml O2 l−1 cause hypoxic stress (Vaquer-Sunyer and Duarte, 2008; Ekau et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: OMZ vertical expansions may alter microbial processes key to nutrient cycling and gas fluxes.
source: OMZ vertical expansions may alter microbial processes key to nutrient cycling and gas fluxes (Levin and Le Bris, 2015), change predator–prey dynamics (Ekau et al., 2010; Stewart et al., 2013), and shift distributions, abundance, and capture risk of ecologically and commercially important species (Ekau et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012; Deutsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: OMZ vertical expansions may change predator–prey dynamics.
source: OMZ vertical expansions may alter microbial processes key to nutrient cycling and gas fluxes (Levin and Le Bris, 2015), change predator–prey dynamics (Ekau et al., 2010; Stewart et al., 2013), and shift distributions, abundance, and capture risk of ecologically and commercially important species (Ekau et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012; Deutsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: OMZ vertical expansions may shift distributions, abundance, and capture risk of ecologically and commercially important species.
source: OMZ vertical expansions may alter microbial processes key to nutrient cycling and gas fluxes (Levin and Le Bris, 2015), change predator–prey dynamics (Ekau et al., 2010; Stewart et al., 2013), and shift distributions, abundance, and capture risk of ecologically and commercially important species (Ekau et al., 2010; Gilly et al., 2013; Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012; Deutsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: OMZ expansion may have significant implications for top predator ecology and fisheries.
source: In particular, OMZ expansion may have significant implications for top predator ecology and fisheries (Gilly et al., 2013; Stramma et al., 2012) since shoaling hypoxic layers are expected to compress the habitat of pelagic fishes (Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Shoaling hypoxic layers are expected to compress the habitat of pelagic fishes.
source: In particular, OMZ expansion may have significant implications for top predator ecology and fisheries (Gilly et al., 2013; Stramma et al., 2012) since shoaling hypoxic layers are expected to compress the habitat of pelagic fishes (Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012; Leung et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Water layers with DO concentrations 3.0–3.5 ml O2 l−1 have been recognised as a generalised lower habitat boundary for large tropical pelagic fishes such as tunas and billfishes.
source: For large tropical pelagic fishes such as tunas and billfishes, water layers with DO concentrations 3.0–3.5 ml O2 l−1 have been recognised as a generalised lower habitat boundary associated with waters overlying OMZs that limits depth distributions (Lowe et al., 2000; Ekau et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The increased susceptibility of large pelagic fishes to fisheries due to shoaling OMZs has been hypothesised but has not been quantified directly.
source: Nonetheless, the increased susceptibility of large pelagic fishes to fisheries due to shoaling OMZs has been hypothesised (Gilly et al., 2013; Prince and Goodyear, 2006; Prince et al., 2010; Stramma et al., 2012) but has not been quantified directly.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the study addresses.

claim: Pelagic sharks are ecologically important oceanic apex predators.
source: Pelagic sharks are ecologically important oceanic apex predators (Hammerschlag et al., 2019) with comparatively high physiological demands for oxygen (Payne et al., 2015) that have been widely observed in the surface layers above OMZs (e.g. Vetter, 2008; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009; Abascal et al., 2011; Queiroz et al., 2016; Queiroz et al., 2019; Sims, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Pelagic sharks have comparatively high physiological demands for oxygen.
source: Pelagic sharks are ecologically important oceanic apex predators (Hammerschlag et al., 2019) with comparatively high physiological demands for oxygen (Payne et al., 2015) that have been widely observed in the surface layers above OMZs (e.g. Vetter, 2008; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009; Abascal et al., 2011; Queiroz et al., 2016; Queiroz et al., 2019; Sims, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Pelagic sharks have been widely observed in the surface layers above OMZs.
source: Pelagic sharks are ecologically important oceanic apex predators (Hammerschlag et al., 2019) with comparatively high physiological demands for oxygen (Payne et al., 2015) that have been widely observed in the surface layers above OMZs (e.g. Vetter, 2008; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009; Abascal et al., 2011; Queiroz et al., 2016; Queiroz et al., 2019; Sims, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: Tens of millions of pelagic sharks are caught each year by largely unregulated fisheries in the high seas.
source: Tens of millions of pelagic sharks are caught each year by largely unregulated fisheries in the high seas (areas beyond national jurisdiction, ABNJ), leading to overfishing and declining catch rates documented for many species (Baum et al., 2003; Ferretti et al., 2010; Worm et al., 2013; Campana, 2016; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2017a; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Pelagic shark fisheries in the high seas are leading to overfishing and declining catch rates documented for many species.
source: Tens of millions of pelagic sharks are caught each year by largely unregulated fisheries in the high seas (areas beyond national jurisdiction, ABNJ), leading to overfishing and declining catch rates documented for many species (Baum et al., 2003; Ferretti et al., 2010; Worm et al., 2013; Campana, 2016; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2017a; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: There has been limited management of commercially important pelagic sharks where OMZs occur in ABNJ.
source: Despite high fishing pressure, there has been limited management of commercially important pelagic sharks where OMZs occur in ABNJ (Campana, 2016; Queiroz et al., 2019), such as for blue Prionace glauca and shortfin mako Isurus oxyrinchus sharks that are the most common sharks caught by Atlantic pelagic fisheries (Queiroz et al., 2016; Oliver et al., 2015; Sims et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Blue sharks and shortfin mako sharks are the most common sharks caught by Atlantic pelagic fisheries.
source: Despite high fishing pressure, there has been limited management of commercially important pelagic sharks where OMZs occur in ABNJ (Campana, 2016; Queiroz et al., 2019), such as for blue Prionace glauca and shortfin mako Isurus oxyrinchus sharks that are the most common sharks caught by Atlantic pelagic fisheries (Queiroz et al., 2016; Oliver et al., 2015; Sims et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The eastern tropical Atlantic OMZ has expanded over the last 50 years.
source: The eastern tropical Atlantic (ETA) OMZ provides an appropriate system to study in this context because expansion of this OMZ has been recorded over the last 50 years, with DO declines there being particularly intense compared to other OMZs (Stramma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: DO declines in the eastern tropical Atlantic OMZ are particularly intense compared to other OMZs.
source: The eastern tropical Atlantic (ETA) OMZ provides an appropriate system to study in this context because expansion of this OMZ has been recorded over the last 50 years, with DO declines there being particularly intense compared to other OMZs (Stramma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: In the ETA OMZ the vertical extent with DO concentrations <2.0 ml O2 l−1 increased in thickness by 85% between 1960 and 2006.
source: For example, in this OMZ the vertical extent with DO concentrations <2.0 ml O2 l−1 – levels known to affect pelagic fish physiology and behaviour (Ekau et al., 2010; Sims, 2019) – increased in thickness by 85% between 1960 and 2006 (Stramma et al., 2008), with more recent observations of exceptionally low DO concentrations of <0.05 ml O2 l−1 ('dead zones') in some ETA mesoscale eddies (Karstensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Exceptionally low DO concentrations of <0.05 ml O2 l−1 ('dead zones') have been observed in some ETA mesoscale eddies.
source: For example, in this OMZ the vertical extent with DO concentrations <2.0 ml O2 l−1 – levels known to affect pelagic fish physiology and behaviour (Ekau et al., 2010; Sims, 2019) – increased in thickness by 85% between 1960 and 2006 (Stramma et al., 2008), with more recent observations of exceptionally low DO concentrations of <0.05 ml O2 l−1 ('dead zones') in some ETA mesoscale eddies (Karstensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: A total of 55 adult or sub-adult blue sharks were tracked in the North Atlantic.
source: A total of 55 adult or sub-adult blue sharks were tracked in the North Atlantic with either an Argos (position only) satellite transmitter or a satellite-linked depth and temperature-recording tag (pop-off satellite archival transmitter, PSAT) (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the sample size of the tracking study.

claim: Of the 22 sharks tagged with Argos transmitters between 2009 and 2014 in fully oxygenated waters adjacent to the ETA OMZ, 10 sharks displayed sustained southern movements of which six utilised waters above the OMZ.
source: Of the 22 sharks tagged with Argos transmitters between 2009 and 2014 in fully oxygenated waters adjacent to the ETA OMZ, 10 sharks displayed sustained southern movements of which six utilised waters above the OMZ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes movement patterns observed in the tracking data.

claim: Five out of six sharks spent significantly more time above the ETA OMZ than respective random models.
source: Five (out of six) sharks spent significantly more time above the ETA OMZ than respective random models (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from statistical comparison with random walk models.

claim: Three sharks (S24, S25, and S27) stayed entirely within the region above the OMZ for the tracking durations (22–40 days).
source: Three sharks (S24, S25, and S27) stayed entirely within the region above the OMZ for the tracking durations (22–40 days), and while seven eventually left the area, two of the seven sharks remained for a significantly longer period than what would be expected by random movements prior to leaving (S23 and S29; tracked for 73 and 125 days, respectively).
evidence: This describes specific tracking results for individual sharks.

claim: Two sharks (S23 and S29) remained in the OMZ area for a significantly longer period than what would be expected by random movements prior to leaving.
source: Three sharks (S24, S25, and S27) stayed entirely within the region above the OMZ for the tracking durations (22–40 days), and while seven eventually left the area, two of the seven sharks remained for a significantly longer period than what would be expected by random movements prior to leaving (S23 and S29; tracked for 73 and 125 days, respectively).
evidence: This is a result from statistical comparison with random walk models.

claim: A vertical shift to shallower depths (increased shoaling) occurred as sharks moved across the core OMZ area compared to dive depths in adjacent (normoxic) waters.
source: A vertical shift to shallower depths (increased shoaling) occurred as sharks moved across the core OMZ area compared to dive depths in adjacent (normoxic) waters (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the dive data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The MDD depths of shark 47 in adjacent waters to the OMZ ranged between 500 and 1400 m, whereas above the core OMZ area MDD depths were 200–520 m.
source: For example, the MDD depths of shark 47 in adjacent waters to the OMZ ranged between 500 and 1400 m, whereas above the core OMZ area MDD depths were 200–520 m (Figure 2A; Table 1).
evidence: This is specific dive depth data for an individual shark.

claim: The deepest MDD depths of shark 52 reached 1480 m in adjacent areas, but were mainly shallower than 250 m in the OMZ (97.6% of time) and only once reached 980 m.
source: Similarly, the deepest MDD depths of shark 52 reached 1480 m in adjacent areas, but were mainly shallower than 250 m in the OMZ (97.6% of time) and only once reached 980 m (Figure 2B; Table 1).
evidence: This is specific dive depth data for an individual shark.

claim: The mean MDD depth reached by individuals that encountered the OMZ was 754 m compared to a mean depth of 1250 m outside the OMZ.
source: Overall, the mean MDD depth reached by individuals that encountered the OMZ was 754 m compared to a mean depth of 1250 m outside the OMZ (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the dive data presented in Table 1.

claim: For all sharks, the mean number of dives >600 m was an order of magnitude lower in waters above the core OMZ than more oxygenated waters outside (mean deep dives per track: above the OMZ = 1.1; adjacent to OMZ area = 10.8).
source: For all sharks, the mean number of dives >600 m was an order of magnitude lower in waters above the core OMZ than more oxygenated waters outside (mean deep dives per track: above the OMZ = 1.1; adjacent to OMZ area = 10.8; Table 1; Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the dive data.

claim: Blue sharks spent 91% of time in depths <250 m in the OMZ area.
source: In addition, it was evident from dive data that although blue sharks undertook dives in the OMZ area (down to 1552 m) potentially taking them through hypoxic water (Figure 3B and D), these were of relatively short duration given that close to 100% of time was spent <500 m (Figures 3A and C and 4), with 91% of time in depths <250 m (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the time-at-depth data.

claim: Sharks tagged outside the OMZ area compared to inside potentially experienced an average decrease in DO from 4.23 ml l−1 to 2.48 ml O2 l−1.
source: Sharks tagged outside the OMZ area compared to inside potentially experienced an average decrease from 4.23 (±0.82 S.D.; minimum of 2.00 ml l−1, maximum of 5.66 ml l−1) to 2.48 ml O2 l−1 (±1.18 S.D.; min. of 1.17 ml l−1, max. of 5.17 ml l−1), corresponding to a decrease in the mean pO2 from 13.39 (±3.08 S.D.; min. of 6.23 kPa, max. of 18.33 kPa) to 8.01 (±4.64 S.D.) kPa, with a minimum of 3.58 kPa and a maximum of 18.37 kPa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from modeled environmental data matched to shark positions.

claim: Almost 100% of shark dive time in the OMZ was spent at depths <500 m even though the sea surface temperatures there were warmer (23–26°C) compared to dive locations outside the OMZ.
source: Almost 100% of shark dive time in the OMZ was spent at depths <500 m even though the sea surface temperatures (SSTs) there were warmer (23–26°C) compared to dive locations outside the OMZ (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the dive and temperature data.

claim: The temperatures encountered vertically by sharks down to MDD depths were similar between the OMZ and normoxic areas (mean ± S.D. OMZ: 15.84 ± 5.18°C; normoxia: 15.75 ± 4.53°C).
source: However, the temperatures encountered vertically by sharks down to MDD depths were similar between the two areas (mean ± S.D. OMZ: 15.84 ± 5.18°C; normoxia: 15.75 ± 4.53°C), down to a minimum of ~5°C (maximum of 26.04°C) in the OMZ and a minimum of ~4°C (maximum of 26.84°C) in normoxia, albeit that these lower temperatures were encountered at shallower depths in the OMZ than outside (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from temperature data at dive depths.

claim: NPP was higher inside the OMZ area than outside.
source: Net primary production (NPP) was higher inside the OMZ area than outside, confirming the known relationship of higher phytoplankton growth in the ETA OMZ area as a consequence of increased stratification and warmer SST above the MLD, and which coincided with greater time spent by blue sharks in the uppermost 150 m water layer (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from environmental data and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peak values of NPP occurred above the MLD at ~100 m depth inside the OMZ, values that were some nine times higher than peak values outside the OMZ in adjacent waters.
source: Peak values of NPP occurred above the MLD at ~100 m depth inside the OMZ, values that were some nine times higher than peak values outside the OMZ in adjacent waters.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of NPP values from environmental data.

claim: MDD depth was best explained by a combination of DO at depth and SST and NPP at depth.
source: Results showed that MDD depth was best explained by a combination of DO at depth and SST and NPP at depth (Table 2).
evidence: This is the result of the GAMM model selection process.

claim: The variables of water temperature at depth, surface salinity and at depth, chlorophyll 'a' and phytoplankton concentration (surface and at depth) did not contribute to the best fit model.
source: The variables of water temperature at depth, surface salinity and at depth, chlorophyll 'a' and phytoplankton concentration (surface and at depth) did not contribute to the best fit model.
evidence: This is the result of the GAMM model selection process.

claim: MDD depth tended to decrease with decreasing DO at depth and SST, and increase with decreasing NPP at depth.
source: Although the relationship between MDD depth and the selected variables in the best fit model was complex, MDD depth tended to decrease with decreasing DO at depth and SST, and increase with decreasing NPP at depth (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the relationships found in the GAMM model.

claim: The decrease in MDD depth was greatest where DO at depth decreased below 3.5 ml l−1.
source: The decrease in MDD depth was greatest where DO at depth decreased below 3.5 ml l−1, whereas above this DO concentration MDD depth was not strongly affected (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes a threshold relationship found in the GAMM model.

claim: Increasing MDD depths occurred with increasing SST up to 24°C; however, in waters with SST above 24°C, MDD depths decreased.
source: Increasing MDD depths occurred with increasing SST up to 24°C; however, in waters with SST above 24°C, which were common above the OMZ (Figure 3B), MDD depths decreased (Figure 6C).
evidence: This describes a non-linear relationship found in the GAMM model.

claim: Fishing effort was higher in the whole North Atlantic when compared to the South Atlantic, with longline fishing vessels spending on average 65 (±74 S.D.) and 30 (±30) fishing effort days per 1 × 1° grid cell, respectively.
source: At the ocean-basin scale, fishing effort (active fishing days with gear deployed) was higher in the whole North Atlantic when compared to the South Atlantic, with longline fishing vessels spending on average 65 (±74 S.D.) and 30 (±30) fishing effort days per 1 × 1° grid cell, respectively (Figure 7; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a summary statistic from the VMS fishing effort data.

claim: At the regional scale in the North Atlantic, fishing effort and fishing intensity were both higher above OMZ areas compared to adjacent waters outside (Mann–Whitney rank sum test, p<0.001).
source: At the regional scale in the North Atlantic, fishing effort and fishing intensity (proportion of total active fishing locations occurring in spatial clusters) were both higher above OMZ areas compared to adjacent waters outside (Mann–Whitney rank sum test, p<0.001; Table 3) (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statistical result from analysis of VMS fishing data.

claim: In the South Atlantic fishing intensity was highest above OMZs.
source: Equally, in the South Atlantic fishing intensity was highest above OMZs (Figure 7; Table 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the VMS fishing data analysis.

claim: Distinct hotspots of fishing effort occurred along the northern, western, and southern boundaries of the OMZ as defined by the oxycline of 3.5 ml O2 l−1 at 100 m depth.
source: Furthermore, it was evident that distinct hotspots of fishing effort occurred along the northern, western, and southern boundaries of the OMZ as defined by the oxycline of 3.5 ml O2 l−1 at 100 m depth (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial distribution of fishing effort shown in Figure 7.

claim: Blue shark catches of Spanish longline vessels showed higher catch per unit effort in the OMZ area compared to adjacent waters further north (>22°N).
source: The blue shark catches of Spanish longline vessels as reported in logbooks showed higher catch per unit effort (CPUE; mean CPUE: kilograms of blue shark caught and retained per grid cell per longline set [day]) in the OMZ area compared to adjacent waters further north (>22°N) which were not affected by hypoxic waters at depth (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the catch data analysis.

claim: A higher number of grid cells with the highest CPUE occurred along the northern boundary of the OMZ (between 15 and 22°N), where there are very strong DO gradients horizontally and vertically.
source: A higher number of grid cells with the highest CPUE occurred along the northern boundary of the OMZ (between 15 and 22°N), where there are very strong DO gradients horizontally and vertically (Figures 1, 2, and 8A and B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the catch data analysis.

claim: CPUE hotspots were evident on the western extent (9–15°N and 30–41°W) and southern boundaries (south of 9°N).
source: CPUE hotspots were also evident on the western extent (9–15°N and 30–41°W) and southern boundaries (south of 9°N) (Figure 8A and C–G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the catch data analysis.

claim: CPUE increased most where DO at 100 m was generally decreasing along transects through the OMZ areas.
source: Examining the fishing-induced blue shark mortality along transects through the OMZ areas showed CPUE increased most where DO at 100 m was generally decreasing (Figure 8B–G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the transect analysis of catch data.

claim: Along the northern boundary (20.5 and 15.5°N transects) CPUE peaked where DO concentration at 100 m decreased most markedly, from ~5 ml O2 l−1 in the west (25–35°W) down to ~1 ml O2 l−1 in the east (15.0–15.5°W).
source: Along the northern boundary (20.5 and 15.5°N transects) CPUE peaked where DO concentration at 100 m decreased most markedly, from ~5 ml O2 l−1 in the west (25–35°W) down to ~1 ml O2 l−1 in the east (15.0–15.5°W).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the transect analysis of catch data.

claim: Along the 20.5°N transect the peak CPUE was estimated to occur where the DO concentration was 3.51 ml O2 l−1.
source: For example, along the 20.5°N transect the peak CPUE was estimated to occur where the DO concentration was 3.51 ml O2 l−1 (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the quadratic model fit to the catch data.

claim: Peak CPUE in individual grid cells occurred along transects where DO concentrations ranged from 1.65 to 3.49 ml O2 l−1.
source: Peak CPUE in individual grid cells occurred along transects where DO concentrations ranged from 1.65 to 3.49 ml O2 l−1 (Table 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the catch data analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: For all CPUE and DO data across grid cells, blue shark CPUE peaked along transects in the OMZ area where DO at 100 m was 2.96 ml O2 l−1.
source: For all CPUE and DO data across grid cells, we estimated that blue shark CPUE peaked along transects in the OMZ area where DO at 100 m was 2.96 ml O2 l−1 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the quadratic model fit to all catch data.

claim: Peak catches of blue shark occurred where sharp gradients in DO were present horizontally and vertically due to shoaling hypoxic water associated with the OMZ.
source: Overall, the results show peak catches of blue shark occurred where sharp gradients in DO were present horizontally and vertically due to shoaling hypoxic water associated with the OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the catch data analysis.

claim: The ETA OMZ environment decreases the vertical range of sharks compared to adjacent waters consistent with the habitat compression hypothesis.
source: Overall, our results show that the ETA OMZ environment decreases the vertical range of sharks compared to adjacent waters consistent with the habitat compression hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: Water temperature at depth did not contribute to the best fit model, indicating that low DO at depth, specific SST values, and high NPP at depths within the uppermost 150 m layer were more important in reducing tracked blue shark MDD depth than gradients in temperature, salinity, and phytoplankton proxies in the water column of the OMZ.
source: Interestingly, we found that water temperature at depth did not contribute to the best fit model, indicating that low DO at depth, specific SST values, and high NPP at depths within the uppermost 150 m layer were more important in reducing tracked blue shark MDD depth than gradients in temperature, salinity, and phytoplankton proxies in the water column of the OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the GAMM model results.

claim: CPUE of blue sharks by longline fishing vessels was higher in the OMZ area, primarily within fishing hotspots along the northern and western edges of the OMZ where the intensity of fishing was significantly higher and where predicted blue shark MDD depths were generally shallower.
source: Furthermore, we found that CPUE of blue sharks by longline fishing vessels was higher in the OMZ area, primarily within fishing hotspots along the northern and western edges of the OMZ where the intensity of fishing was significantly higher and where predicted blue shark MDD depths were generally shallower.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the fishing and catch data analysis.

claim: The blue shark is probably the ocean's widest ranging shark with documented individual movements of thousands of kilometres across entire ocean basins and from the surface down to over 1600 m depth.
source: The blue shark is probably the ocean's widest ranging shark with documented individual movements of thousands of kilometres across entire ocean basins and from the surface down to over 1600 m depth (Vandeperre et al., 2014; Queiroz et al., 2017; Queiroz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Blue sharks are capable of tolerating a very broad range of environmental conditions, such as water temperatures between 4°C and 30°C.
source: Blue sharks in the course of these extensive movements encounter and appear capable of tolerating a very broad range of environmental conditions, such as water temperatures between 4°C and 30°C (Howey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The average maximum dive depth of tracked blue sharks in the ETA OMZ was 40% less than the mean depth attained outside the area.
source: Despite this, we found that the average maximum dive depth of tracked blue sharks in the ETA OMZ was 40% less than the mean depth attained outside the area, together with a greatly reduced frequency of deep diving below 600 m inside the OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the dive data analysis.

claim: There was only a relatively small increase (6%) in the time spent in the upper 250 m layer when sharks were inside the OMZ area compared to outside it.
source: In contrast, there was only a relatively small increase (6%) in the time spent in the upper 250 m layer when sharks were inside the OMZ area compared to outside it.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the time-at-depth data analysis.

claim: Limitation of the vertical extent of deep dives in OMZ areas compared to adjacent areas was also apparent for white sharks and shortfin mako sharks along the northern and southern edges of the eastern Pacific OMZ.
source: Limitation of the vertical extent of deep dives in OMZ areas compared to adjacent areas was also apparent for white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009) and shortfin mako sharks (Isurus oxyrinchus; Abascal et al., 2011) along the northern and southern edges of the eastern Pacific OMZ, respectively.
evidence: This is stated with citation support to compare with findings from other species.

claim: The lower DO habitat boundary for blue shark was estimated to be ~3.5 ml O2 l−1 at ~18°C.
source: Considering DO concentrations, the GAMM results indicate a lower DO habitat boundary – defined here as the DO concentration below which MDD depth becomes more limited by further decreases in oxygen content – that was estimated by our model to be ~3.5 ml O2 l−1 at ~18°C.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the GAMM model analysis.

claim: The lower habitat boundary DO concentration for blue shark is consistent with studies showing depth distributions of yellowfin and skipjack tunas are limited by reductions in oxygen content to only 3.5 ml O2 l−1.
source: The lower habitat boundary DO concentration we found for blue shark is consistent with studies showing depth distributions of yellowfin (Thunnus albacares) and skipjack (Katsuwonus pelamis) tunas are limited by reductions in oxygen content to only 3.5 ml O2 l−1 (Gooding et al., 1981; Cayré and Marsac, 1993; Richard, 1994; Lowe et al., 2000).
evidence: This compares the study findings with previous research on tunas.

claim: The minimum oxygen conditions potentially encountered by blue sharks were estimated to be 3.58–4.27 kPa at 12–18°C.
source: For blue sharks, we estimated from modelled oxygen concentrations during vertical movements that the minimum oxygen conditions potentially encountered were 3.58–4.27 kPa at 12–18°C, suggesting blue sharks enter waters with low partial pressures of oxygen that in many fish species, including benthic sharks, would be oxygen levels that elicit oxyconforming responses (Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is calculated from modeled environmental data matched to shark dive depths.

claim: Blue sharks appear able to utilise low DO environments associated with the ETA OMZ for short time periods.
source: Therefore, whilst blue sharks appear able to utilise low DO environments associated with the ETA OMZ for short time periods, our results overall indicate that the OMZ habitat reduced MDD depths and the frequency at which deep MDD depths were reached.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the dive data.

claim: Tracking-based estimates of potential hypoxic thresholds with DO concentrations of 1.2–3.5 ml O2 l−1 for blue sharks also generally limit the dive depths of other pelagic sharks.
source: However, tracking-based estimates of potential hypoxic thresholds with DO concentrations of 1.2–3.5 ml O2 l−1 that we estimated for blue sharks also generally limit the dive depths of other pelagic sharks (Vetter, 2008; Abascal et al., 2011; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009).
evidence: This compares the study findings with previous research on other shark species.

claim: Shortfin mako sharks near the eastern tropical Pacific OMZ generally remained in waters with >3 ml O2 l−1 and rarely encountered water with <2 ml O2 l−1.
source: For example, studies tracking shortfin mako (I. oxyrinchus) near the eastern tropical Pacific (ETP) OMZ indicated individuals generally remained in waters with >3 ml O2 l−1 and rarely encountered water with <2 ml O2 l−1 (Vetter, 2008; Abascal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: White sharks offshore in the ETP were typically associated with DO concentrations of >3 ml O2 l−1.
source: Similarly, white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) offshore in the ETP were typically associated with DO concentrations of >3 ml O2 l−1 (Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009), and salmon sharks (Lamna ditropis) in the eastern North Pacific were found to exploit low DO environments of <3 ml O2 l−1 (Coffey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Salmon sharks in the eastern North Pacific were found to exploit low DO environments of <3 ml O2 l−1.
source: Similarly, white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) offshore in the ETP were typically associated with DO concentrations of >3 ml O2 l−1 (Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009), and salmon sharks (Lamna ditropis) in the eastern North Pacific were found to exploit low DO environments of <3 ml O2 l−1 (Coffey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Blue sharks may occasionally enter low DO waters (<1.5 ml O2 l−1).
source: Our study also showed blue sharks may occasionally enter low DO waters (<1.5 ml O2 l−1), which is proposed for other pelagic shark species (Vetter, 2008; Abascal et al., 2011; Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the dive data with citation support for similar findings in other species.

claim: The overall picture emerging from tracking sharks in relation to modelled DO is that vertical extent is limited by low DO, with a general lower habitat boundary around 3.5 ml O2 l−1 but with shorter duration deeper dives into more hypoxic water possible.
source: The overall picture emerging from tracking sharks in relation to modelled DO, including this study, is that vertical extent is limited by low DO, with a general lower habitat boundary around 3.5 ml O2 l−1 but with shorter duration deeper dives into more hypoxic water possible.
evidence: This is stated as a synthesis of findings from this and previous studies.

claim: The combination of water temperature and DO has been shown to be an important constraint affecting vertical range of fish including pelagic sharks.
source: In previous studies of fish including pelagic sharks, the combination of water temperature and DO has been shown to an important constraint affecting vertical range (Nasby-Lucas et al., 2009; Abascal et al., 2011; Coffey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Higher water temperatures decrease oxygen solubility, and consequently, available environmental pO2.
source: Hypoxia tolerance represents the minimum environmental pO2 (Pcrit) with which an individual can regulate oxygen uptake (Farrell and Richards, 2009) and higher water temperatures decrease oxygen solubility, and consequently, available environmental pO2 (Tromans, 1998; Garcia, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The MDD depth of the salmon shark tracked in the northeast Pacific Ocean decreased when waters with low DO (<1–3 ml l−1) and cold temperatures (<6°C) at depth were encountered, with both factors contributing to the best fit GAMM.
source: In a recent study, the MDD depth of the salmon shark tracked with satellite archival transmitters in the northeast Pacific Ocean decreased when waters with low DO (<1–3 ml l−1) and cold temperatures (<6°C) at depth were encountered, with both factors contributing to the best fit GAMM (Coffey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation support to compare with findings from another species.

claim: Blue sharks were not solely limited in MDD depth by temperature at depth because the temperatures encountered in the OMZ (5–26°C) were within their normal, wide temperature range recorded in other studies.
source: The temperatures encountered by blue sharks in the OMZ (5–26°C) were within their normal, wide temperature range recorded in other studies (Queiroz et al., 2012; Howey et al., 2017), which suggests that the individuals we tracked were not solely limited in MDD depth by temperature at depth.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the temperature data with citation support.

claim: SST has been shown in previous studies to be an important factor determining the habitat preferences of blue sharks in the North Atlantic.
source: SST has been shown in previous studies to be an important factor determining the habitat preferences of blue sharks in the North Atlantic (Queiroz et al., 2016), so it was expected that SST would contribute to the best fit model.
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The ETA OMZ is characterised by higher SSTs than adjacent waters.
source: The ETA OMZ is characterised by higher SSTs than adjacent waters (e.g. Figure 2A) and, indeed, we found that MDD depth increased with increasing SST up to 24°C, with SST >24°C being observed along blue shark tracks across the core OMZ area that coincided with the shallowest MDD depths.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the environmental data.

claim: The combination of high SST above the OMZ lowering oxygen solubility in water, together with the increased metabolic costs of an ectothermic shark associated with occupying elevated SSTs, may have acted to reduce the tolerance of blue sharks to undertake deeper dives into waters with low DO at depth.
source: The combination of high SST above the OMZ lowering oxygen solubility in water, together with the increased metabolic costs (oxygen consumption) of an ectothermic shark such as the blue shark associated with occupying elevated SSTs (Payne et al., 2015), may have acted to reduce the tolerance of blue sharks to undertake deeper dives into waters with low DO at depth.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism with citation support.

claim: The seasonal increase in phytoplankton abundance on the northeast-Atlantic continental shelf edge occurs a few weeks before an increase in zooplankton abundance and the occurrence of zooplankton-feeding basking sharks.
source: For example, the seasonal increase in phytoplankton abundance on the northeast-Atlantic continental shelf edge occurs a few weeks before an increase in zooplankton abundance and the occurrence of zooplankton-feeding basking sharks (Cetorhinus maximus) (Sims et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation support as an example of biological resource effects on predator habitat selection.

claim: The highest NPP concentrations in the ETA OMZ area occurred in the uppermost 150 m layer above the core OMZ.
source: However, in the ETA OMZ area, the highest NPP concentrations occurred in the uppermost 150 m layer above the core OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the environmental data.

claim: The combined effects of low DO at depth and higher basal biomass in the upper layer above the core OMZ may lead to enhanced shark–prey interactions in the surface layers.
source: The combined effects of low DO at depth and higher basal biomass in the upper layer above the core OMZ may lead to enhanced shark–prey interactions in the surface layers.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Some tracked blue sharks (10 of 16; 63%) exhibited selection of habitats above the core OMZ when encountered.
source: Results support the hypothesis that some tracked blue sharks (10 of 16; 63%) exhibited selection of habitats above the core OMZ when encountered, which could be explained by enhanced foraging opportunities for sharks above and possibly within low DO environments of the OMZ that occurred in the uppermost 150 m layer.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the tracking data analysis.

claim: Expanding OMZs due to climate change (shoaling low DO; increasing SST and higher upper layer NPP) will cause habitat compression of blue sharks further into surface waters above expanding OMZs and reduce habitat volumes.
source: Therefore, overall, our results support the hypothesis that expanding OMZs due to climate change (shoaling low DO; increasing SST and higher upper layer NPP) will cause habitat compression of blue sharks further into surface waters above expanding OMZs and reduce habitat volumes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Abiotic (low DO and high SST) and biotic factors (NPP, hence fish prey species) contribute to the observed decreased MDD depth of blue sharks in the ETA OMZ.
source: The results strongly suggest that abiotic (low DO and high SST) and biotic factors (NPP, hence fish prey species) contribute to the observed decreased MDD depth of blue sharks in the ETA OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Habitat compression suggests blue sharks will be increasingly at risk of capture by surface fisheries as a consequence of further deoxygenation of waters deeper than the surface mixed layer overlying the OMZ.
source: This habitat compression suggests blue sharks will be increasingly at risk of capture by surface fisheries as a consequence of further deoxygenation of waters deeper than the surface mixed (oxygenated) layer overlying the OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the study findings.

claim: The potential susceptibility (availability and encounterability risks) of sharks to baited longline hook depths above OMZs are likely to be higher in the future due to habitat compression expected in surface waters from climate-driven OMZ expansion.
source: The habitat compression expected in surface waters due to climate-driven OMZ expansion and its concomitant effects on prey species distributions predicts that the potential susceptibility (availability and encounterability risks) of sharks to baited longline hook depths above OMZs are likely to be higher in the future.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the study findings.

claim: A limitation of this study was that modelled DO data from oceanographic data sets were matched with locations along the paths of tracked pelagic sharks.
source: A limitation of this study was that modelled DO data from oceanographic data sets were matched with locations along the paths of tracked pelagic sharks (Sims, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: Actual DO concentrations in the habitats selected by sharks may differ from interpolated, modelled DO values.
source: Actual DO concentrations in the habitats selected by sharks may therefore differ from interpolated, modelled DO values.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty from using modeled data.

claim: There is a need for direct DO measurements to assess more accurately how pelagic sharks' movements may be limited by low DO levels in the wild.
source: There is a need for direct DO measurements to assess more accurately how pelagic sharks' movements may be limited by low DO levels in the wild.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for future research.

claim: Data-logging tags capable of measuring DO and swimming depths have been developed for recording DO levels that are directly encountered by free-ranging marine predators including large sharks.
source: Data-logging tags capable of measuring DO and swimming depths have been developed for recording DO levels that are directly encountered by free-ranging marine predators (Bailleul et al., 2015) including large sharks (Coffey and Holland, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Oxygen saturations as low as 9.4% of normoxia (~0.8 ml O2 l−1 at 5°C) were recorded from tags on bluntnose sixgill sharks off Hawaii during dives to nearly 700 m depth.
source: Oxygen saturations as low as 9.4% of normoxia (~0.8 ml O2 l−1 at 5°C) were recorded from tags on bluntnose sixgill sharks (Hexanchus griseus) off Hawaii, Pacific Ocean, during dives to nearly 700 m depth (Coffey and Holland, 2015; Coffey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: DO sensor tag results confirm that very low DO concentrations are encountered and can be tolerated by large sharks during normal vertical movement.
source: DO sensor tag results to date confirm that very low DO concentrations are encountered and can be tolerated by large sharks during normal vertical movement.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous research with DO sensor tags.

claim: The model output predicting how the OMZ environment affects blue shark vertical habitat suggests the susceptibility to capture by fisheries will be increased in areas where the DO shoals the most to further reduce vertical extent.
source: The model output predicting how the OMZ environment affects blue shark vertical habitat suggests the susceptibility to capture by fisheries will be increased in areas where the DO shoals the most to further reduce vertical extent.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the model results.

claim: Fishing effort and blue shark CPUE were highest in the same discrete areas (hotspots) along the northern, western, and southern boundaries of the ETA OMZ, indicating both higher fishing intensity and capture success in those areas with greatest reduction in blue shark MDD depth.
source: This assertion was broadly supported in this study by the empirical fishing effort and catch data. This showed that fishing effort and blue shark CPUE were highest in the same discrete areas (hotspots) along the northern, western, and southern boundaries of the ETA OMZ, indicating both higher fishing intensity and capture success in those areas with greatest reduction in blue shark MDD depth.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the fishing and catch data analysis.

claim: Longline fishing patterns above the ETA OMZ form among the most important fishing hotspots within the entire eastern Atlantic.
source: The results indicate longline fishing patterns above the ETA OMZ form among the most important fishing hotspots within the entire eastern Atlantic, particularly along the northern extent of the ETA OMZ.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the fishing effort data.

claim: Higher fishing intensity in the OMZ area indicates that vessels spend less time searching for, or moving to, different fishing locations.
source: Furthermore, higher fishing intensity in the OMZ area indicates that vessels spend less time searching for, or moving to, different fishing locations.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the fishing intensity metric.

claim: Vessels above the OMZ deploy longlines nearly continuously (daily) in localised areas rather than having to interrupt fishing by travelling for days between fishing hotspots.
source: As a result, vessels above the OMZ deploy longlines nearly continuously (daily) in localised areas rather than having to interrupt fishing by travelling for days between fishing hotspots (Queiroz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the fishing intensity data with citation support.

claim: Areas of high fishing intensity are likely known to fishers from previous experience to be fishing hotspots supporting higher large fish catches.
source: These areas of high fishing intensity are likely known to fishers from previous experience to be fishing hotspots supporting higher large fish catches (Queiroz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an inference with citation support.

claim: Blue shark CPUE by Spanish longlines peaked where the modelled DO concentrations at 100 m were in the range 3.0–3.5 ml O2 l−1.
source: Our results showed blue shark CPUE by Spanish longlines peaked where the modelled DO concentrations at 100 m were in the range 3.0–3.5 ml O2 l−1 (Supplementary file 1), which is a similar concentration range to a lower-habitat-boundary DO concentration of ~3.5 ml O2 l−1 that we determined from the GAMM (with tracking-derived MDD depth as the response variable).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the catch data analysis.

claim: The similarity of DO concentration ranges between peak CPUE and the lower habitat boundary suggests blue sharks begin being limited in vertical extent by the 3.5 ml l−1 DO surface (oxycline).
source: The similarity of these ranges suggests a potential mechanism underlying the peak catches observed. Here, blue sharks begin being limited in vertical extent by the 3.5 ml l−1 DO surface (oxycline).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the comparison of CPUE and model results.

claim: Where there is a strong gradient between the preferred DO surface and deeper, less oxygenated waters, the movements of sharks along the more suitable oxygen gradients may lead to aggregation along the boundary of the hypoxic zone.
source: Where there is a strong gradient between this preferred DO surface and deeper, less oxygenated waters, the movements of sharks along the more suitable oxygen gradients may therefore lead to aggregation along the boundary of the hypoxic zone.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Previous studies on fish and invertebrates near low oxygen environments have reported higher mean catches, or steep increases in catches, relative to lower DO values.
source: Previous studies on fish and invertebrates near low oxygen environments have reported higher mean catches, or steep increases in catches, relative to lower DO values (Howell and Simpson, 1994; Song et al., 2009; Ekau et al., 2010; Craig, 2012; Potier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The effects of hypoxia avoidance by brown shrimp and several demersal fish species in the Gulf of Mexico resulted in evading organisms aggregating short distances of 1–3 km just beyond the margins of the hypoxic zone.
source: For example, the effects of hypoxia avoidance by brown shrimp (Farfantepanaeus aztecus) and several demersal fish species in the Gulf of Mexico resulted in evading organisms aggregating short distances of 1–3 km just beyond the margins of the hypoxic zone and in a narrow region along the hypoxic edge (Craig, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Several species of tunas frequently diving below the thermocline show a vertical compression to shallow depths in the presence of an OMZ.
source: Likewise, several species of tunas frequently diving below the thermocline show a vertical compression to shallow depths in the presence of an OMZ (Richard, 1994; Song et al., 2009; Potier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Increased occurrence of tunas in well-oxygenated waters above OMZs increases the overlap between tuna vertical distribution and depths of gear deployments of surface longline fishing hooks and purse seiners.
source: Consequently, increased occurrence in well-oxygenated waters above OMZs increases the overlap between tuna vertical distribution and depths of gear deployments of surface longline fishing hooks and purse seiners (Richard, 1994; Song et al., 2009; Potier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The increased vulnerability of tunas to fisheries in OMZs is in line with the observed higher catches of tunas within these areas.
source: The increased vulnerability of tunas to fisheries in OMZs is in line with the observed higher catches of tunas within these areas (Song et al., 2009; Potier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: The peak catches of blue sharks observed in association with strong DO gradients may have resulted from movements limited by and aggregated along and above the boundary-edge oxycline, which may also have aggregated prey species.
source: Similarly, the peak catches of blue sharks we observed in association with strong DO gradients may have resulted from movements limited by and, hence, aggregated along and above this boundary-edge oxycline, which may also have aggregated prey species, thus leading to higher use of these areas by blue sharks.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism.

claim: Blue sharks above the ETA OMZ will undergo habitat compression as they respond by avoiding lower DO concentrations and associating with high SST and NPP in the uppermost 100 m layer.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that blue sharks above the ETA OMZ will undergo habitat compression as they respond by avoiding lower DO concentrations and associating with high SST and NPP in the uppermost 100 m layer, and show preference for suitable DO gradients along the margins of OMZ areas – potentially due to the physiological limits of sharks (Payne et al., 2015; Coffey et al., 2017; Sims, 2019), to habitat compression of prey species (Gilly et al., 2013; Childress and Seibel, 1998), or even hypoxia-related visual impairment (McCormick and Levin, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion with citation support.

claim: Blue sharks show preference for suitable DO gradients along the margins of OMZ areas potentially due to the physiological limits of sharks, habitat compression of prey species, or hypoxia-related visual impairment.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that blue sharks above the ETA OMZ will undergo habitat compression as they respond by avoiding lower DO concentrations and associating with high SST and NPP in the uppermost 100 m layer, and show preference for suitable DO gradients along the margins of OMZ areas – potentially due to the physiological limits of sharks (Payne et al., 2015; Coffey et al., 2017; Sims, 2019), to habitat compression of prey species (Gilly et al., 2013; Childress and Seibel, 1998), or even hypoxia-related visual impairment (McCormick and Levin, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism with citation support.

claim: These responses combine to further increase shark risk of capture by surface fisheries as OMZs expand given that longline fisheries already target specific OMZ habitats where increased shark catches are made.
source: Our results propose that these responses combine to further increase shark risk of capture by surface fisheries as OMZs expand given that longline fisheries already target specific OMZ habitats where increased shark catches are made.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study findings.

claim: The blue shark makes up ~90% of the total reported catch of pelagic sharks in the Atlantic.
source: The blue shark makes up ~90% of the total reported catch of pelagic sharks in the Atlantic (Oliver et al., 2015) and its fins are those most commonly traded in international markets (Fields et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Blue shark fins are those most commonly traded in international markets.
source: The blue shark makes up ~90% of the total reported catch of pelagic sharks in the Atlantic (Oliver et al., 2015) and its fins are those most commonly traded in international markets (Fields et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Reporting of blue shark catches remains poor.
source: Reporting of catches remains poor, however (Campana, 2016), despite uncertainty about blue shark stock status (e.g. North Atlantic; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2017a; International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citation support.

claim: Blue shark habitat will become further compressed above OMZs in the future due to ongoing ocean deoxygenation.
source: Our study predicts that blue shark habitat will not only become further compressed above OMZs in the future due to ongoing ocean deoxygenation (Breitburg et al., 2018), but, as a consequence, this species will become more susceptible to capture due to higher fishing intensity leading to higher CPUE than in more oxygenated adjacent areas.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the study with citation support.

claim: Blue sharks will become more susceptible to capture due to higher fishing intensity leading to higher CPUE than in more oxygenated adjacent areas as a consequence of habitat compression.
source: Our study predicts that blue shark habitat will not only become further compressed above OMZs in the future due to ongoing ocean deoxygenation (Breitburg et al., 2018), but, as a consequence, this species will become more susceptible to capture due to higher fishing intensity leading to higher CPUE than in more oxygenated adjacent areas.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the study.

claim: Management measures for threatened pelagic sharks, which specifically act to mitigate the effects of ocean deoxygenation on catch rates, may be required as oceans continue warming.
source: Management measures for threatened pelagic sharks, which specifically act to mitigate the effects of ocean deoxygenation on catch rates, may be required as oceans continue warming.
evidence: This is stated as a management recommendation.

claim: Spatial management, such as high-seas large marine protected areas around an OMZ, may be a management option necessary to consider in the warmer deoxygenating oceans of the future.
source: Spatial management, such as high-seas large marine protected areas (LMPAs) around an OMZ for example, may be a management option necessary to consider in the warmer deoxygenating oceans of the future in addition to the need for more effective existing catch control measures to conserve shark populations.
evidence: This is stated as a management recommendation.
